answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Stein line. It appears verbatim in her essay “Reflection on the Atom Bomb,” written in 1946 and first published in the Yale Poetry Review (December 1947), where it is immediately followed by “They listen so much that they forget to be natural.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Reflection on the Atomic Bomb, ed. Robert Bartlett Haas (Black Sparrow Press, 1973)

source.excerpt: I am not so scared, there is so much to be scared of so what is the use of bothering to be scared, and if you are not scared the atomic bomb is not interesting. Everybody gets so much information all day long that they lose their common sense. They listen so much that they forget to be natural.
trail: The full essay text at the University of Pennsylvania contains the sentence verbatim, in context.
Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced section, citing “Reflections on the Atom Bomb” (1946).
WIST Quotations documents the citation as “Reflection on the Atomic Bomb” (1946), Yale Poetry Review (Dec 1947).
source.excerptNote: The famous line is the second sentence; it is almost always quoted alone, stripped of both the atomic-bomb framing and the sentence that finishes the thought.

source.rightsNote: Stein wrote the essay in 1946 and it was first published posthumously in the Yale Poetry Review in December 1947. Under U.S. law a work first published in 1947 remains in copyright, so the wording is controlled by Stein’s estate and its publishers, not public domain.

author.name: Gertrude Stein
author.heading: About Gertrude Stein
author.bio: Gertrude Stein was an American writer who spent most of her life in Paris, where her salon at 27 rue de Fleurus was a hub of modernist art and letters. Known for radically experimental prose and repetitions — “Rose is a rose is a rose is a rose” — she wrote The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas and mentored a generation of writers. “Reflection on the Atom Bomb” was one of her final pieces, written the year she died.

misattribution.heading: A genuine quote, often mangled
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Stein. What goes wrong is the wording and the context.

items.why: Stein wrote “Everybody,” not “Everyone.” The primary text reads “Everybody gets so much information all day long…”; the “Everyone” version circulates widely on quote sites but is not what she wrote.

The line is almost always presented as a timeless remark about digital information overload. In fact it comes from a 1946 reflection on the atomic bomb, and its next sentence — “They listen so much that they forget to be natural” — is usually dropped.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: authentically Gertrude Stein, from “Reflection on the Atom Bomb” (1946) — just spell it “Everybody” and remember it was written under the shadow of the bomb, per the sourced record.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Asked in 1946 what she thought of the atomic bomb, Stein answered that she could not take any interest in it — the essay is a study in deliberate un-alarm. The common-sense line is her diagnosis of the surrounding noise: not the bomb, but the flood of talk and information around it, is what leaves people unable to think plainly.

Written months before her death, the piece reads as one of her last aphoristic verdicts on modern life, which is partly why the sentence has outlived its atomic-age occasion and been adopted, almost verbatim, as a motto for the information age.
